"title": "Highly sensitive and full-genome interrogation of SARS-CoV-2 using multiplexed PCR enrichment followed by next-generation sequencing",
"authors": "Chenyu Li, David N Debruyne, Julia Spencer, Vidushi Kapoor, Lily Y Liu, Bo Zhou, Utsav Pandey, Moiz Bootwalla, Dejerianne Ostrow, Dennis T Maglinte, David Ruble, Alex Ryutov, Lishuang Shen, Lucie Lee, Rounak Feigelman, Grayson Burdon, Jeffrey Liu, Alejandra Oliva, Adam Borcherding, Hongdong Tan, Alexander E Urban, Xiaowu Gai, Jennifer Dien Bard, Guoying Liu, Zhitong Liu",
"field_subfield": "Molecular diagnostics / clinical genomics (SARS-CoV-2 detection and surveillance)",
"type_of_paper": "Methods development and validation study",
"executive_summary": "This study addresses a central weakness of the standard reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) for SARS-CoV-2: although RT-PCR is the most commonly used diagnostic method because of its high sensitivity, typically claiming detection of about 5 copies of viruses, it has been reported that only 47-59% of the positive cases were identified by some RT-PCR methods, probably due to low viral load, timing of sampling, degradation of virus RNA in the sampling process, or possible mutations spanning the primer binding sites. The authors therefore developed a multiplex-PCR-based method comprised of 343 pairs of specific primers to improve sensitivity and accommodate various application settings. The assay produced clean characteristic target peaks of defined sizes, which allowed for direct identification of positives by electrophoresis. Using a mathematical model of RT-PCR, the authors estimated that RT-PCR assays could only detect 4.8 copies of SARS-CoV-2 at 95% probability, with a predicted probability of detecting one copy of only 26%. In contrast, their multiplex PCR panel of 172 primer pairs was estimated to detect 1.15 copies at 95% probability, and the two overlapping pools together achieved a calculated detection limit of 0.29 copies at 95% probability. Experimentally, the method detected SARS-CoV-2 at low copy numbers, with a wide dynamic range from 1 to about 1,000 copies of plasmids, and approximately 96% of the amplicons were recovered with 14 copies of plasmids. The authors amplified the entire SARS-CoV-2 genome from 8 to half a million viral copies purified from 13 COVID-19 positive specimens, and detected mutations through next generation sequencing on the Illumina MiSeq. They found a correlation between genome coverage and viral copy number, with about 95% of the genome covered at 100X for 8 copies of virus. Mutations were detected from samples with viral loads ranging from 8 to half a million copies, and the majority clustered around 7 loci. The D614G mutation was found in 11 of these 13 specimens. Finally, the authors developed a multiplex-PCR-based metagenomic method that required modest sequencing depth for uncovering SARS-CoV-2 mutational diversity and potentially novel or emerging isolates, achieving >96% coverage of the S and N genes of SARS-CoV-2 in the context of human gDNA while only requiring ~0.6M of total reads per library. This coverage was superior given the recommended 50% threshold of coverage for drafting a genome. The results were obtained with no additional means of host depletion to remove human gDNA and rRNA. The viral bases were 16% of the total recovered bases in the sequencing. The study demonstrates that multiplex PCR is more sensitive than RT-PCR and tolerates the presence of mutations in SARS-CoV-2, and that the method could be further expanded to include simultaneous detection of other respiratory viruses including influenza virus. The paper provides a highly sensitive and robust multiplex PCR method for the detection of SARS-CoV-2, and establishes a user-friendly multiplex-PCR-based metagenomic method that could also be applied for the identification of novel pathogens with a moderate sequencing depth of approximately 1 million reads.",

summary.title: Highly sensitive and full-genome interrogation of SARS-CoV-2 using multiplexed PCR enrichment followed by next-generation sequencing
summary.authors: Chenyu Li, David N Debruyne, Julia Spencer, Vidushi Kapoor, Lily Y Liu, Bo Zhou, Utsav Pandey, Moiz Bootwalla, Dejerianne Ostrow, Dennis T Maglinte, David Ruble, Alex Ryutov, Lishuang Shen, Lucie Lee, Rounak Feigelman, Grayson Burdon, Jeffrey Liu, Alejandra Oliva, Adam Borcherding, Hongdong Tan, Alexander E Urban, Xiaowu Gai, Jennifer Dien Bard, Guoying Liu, Zhitong Liu
summary.field_subfield: Molecular diagnostics / clinical genomics (SARS-CoV-2 detection and surveillance)
summary.executive_summary: This study addresses a central weakness of the standard reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) for SARS-CoV-2: although RT-PCR is the most commonly used diagnostic method because of its high sensitivity, typically claiming detection of about 5 copies of viruses, it has been reported that only 47-59% of the positive cases were identified by some RT-PCR methods, probably due to low viral load, timing of sampling, degradation of virus RNA in the sampling process, or possible mutations spanning the primer binding sites. The authors therefore developed a multiplex-PCR-based method comprised of 343 pairs of specific primers to improve sensitivity and accommodate various application settings. The assay produced clean characteristic target peaks of defined sizes, which allowed for direct identification of positives by electrophoresis. Using a mathematical model of RT-PCR, the authors estimated that RT-PCR assays could only detect 4.8 copies of SARS-CoV-2 at 95% probability, with a predicted probability of detecting one copy of only 26%. In contrast, their multiplex PCR panel of 172 primer pairs was estimated to detect 1.15 copies at 95% probability, and the two overlapping pools together achieved a calculated detection limit of 0.29 copies at 95% probability. Experimentally, the method detected SARS-CoV-2 at low copy numbers, with a wide dynamic range from 1 to about 1,000 copies of plasmids, and approximately 96% of the amplicons were recovered with 14 copies of plasmids. The authors amplified the entire SARS-CoV-2 genome from 8 to half a million viral copies purified from 13 COVID-19 positive specimens, and detected mutations through next generation sequencing on the Illumina MiSeq. They found a correlation between genome coverage and viral copy number, with about 95% of the genome covered at 100X for 8 copies of virus. Mutations were detected from samples with viral loads ranging from 8 to half a million copies, and the majority clustered around 7 loci. The D614G mutation was found in 11 of these 13 specimens. Finally, the authors developed a multiplex-PCR-based metagenomic method that required modest sequencing depth for uncovering SARS-CoV-2 mutational diversity and potentially novel or emerging isolates, achieving >96% coverage of the S and N genes of SARS-CoV-2 in the context of human gDNA while only requiring ~0.6M of total reads per library. This coverage was superior given the recommended 50% threshold of coverage for drafting a genome. The results were obtained with no additional means of host depletion to remove human gDNA and rRNA. The viral bases were 16% of the total recovered bases in the sequencing. The study demonstrates that multiplex PCR is more sensitive than RT-PCR and tolerates the presence of mutations in SARS-CoV-2, and that the method could be further expanded to include simultaneous detection of other respiratory viruses including influenza virus. The paper provides a highly sensitive and robust multiplex PCR method for the detection of SARS-CoV-2, and establishes a user-friendly multiplex-PCR-based metagenomic method that could also be applied for the identification of novel pathogens with a moderate sequencing depth of approximately 1 million reads.

The authors amplified the entire SARS-CoV-2 genome from 8 to half a million viral copies purified from 13 COVID-19 positive specimens, and detected mutations through next generation sequencing on the Illumina MiSeq. They found a correlation between genome coverage and viral copy number, with about 95% of the genome covered at 100X for 8 copies of virus. Mutations were detected from samples with viral loads ranging from 8 to half a million copies, and the majority clustered around 7 loci. The D614G mutation was found in 11 of these 13 specimens. This coverage was superior given the recommended 50% threshold of coverage for drafting a genome. The results were obtained with no additional means of host depletion to remove human gDNA and rRNA. The viral bases were 16% of the total recovered bases in the sequencing. The study demonstrates that multiplex PCR is more sensitive than RT-PCR and tolerates the presence of mutations in SARS-CoV-2, and that the method could be further expanded to include simultaneous detection of other respiratory viruses including influenza virus. The paper provides a highly sensitive and robust multiplex PCR method for the detection of SARS-CoV-2, and establishes a user-friendly multiplex-PCR-based metagenomic method that could also be applied for the identification of novel pathogens with a moderate sequencing depth of approximately 1 million reads.

Research Context
RT-PCR is the most commonly used method for COVID-19 diagnosis and surveillance. RT-PCR is considered the gold standard because of its ease of use and high sensitivity. Only 47-59% of true positive cases were identified by RT-PCR. 75% of RT-PCR negative results were later found positive with other assays. Low detection may result from low viral load, sampling timing, RNA degradation, or primer-binding mutations. Full-length genome sequencing is essential for surveillance of SARS-CoV-2 evolution. Multiplex PCR has high coverage, specificity, and sensitivity for other pathogens. Metagenomic approaches require very high sequencing depth and are economically prohibitive.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether multiplex PCR can outperform RT-PCR in sensitivity. The hypothesis is that multiplex PCR has significantly higher sensitivity than RT-PCR. Multiplex PCR may detect fragments from degraded viral genomes and tolerate genomic variations. The method should distinguish SARS-CoV-2 from other respiratory pathogens. Full genome sequencing should enable surveillance of SARS-CoV-2 evolution. A metagenomic method should detect novel pathogens at moderate sequencing depth. The predicted outcome is a calculated detection limit of 0.29 copies at 95% probability. The predicted outcome is >96% coverage of the S and N genes with ~0.6M reads.

Methodological Details
The study was conducted by Paragon Genomics Inc and Stanford University collaborators. The SARS-CoV-2 genome size used for modeling was 29,903bp (NC_045512.2). A panel of 172 pairs of multiplex PCR primers was designed. The average amplicon length was 99bp with a 76±10bp gap between adjacent amplicons. A second pool of 171 primer pairs overlapped with the first pool. The two overlapping pools provide full coverage of the entire viral genome. Two plasmids containing the S and N genes were used to validate the method. Plasmids were spiked into cDNA from human total RNA to simulate clinical samples. Copy number was determined by droplet-based digital PCR (ddPCR) with a QX200 system from Bio-Rad. Plasmids were diluted from approximately 9,000 copies to below one copy. The multiplex PCR products were further amplified in a secondary PCR. Sample indexes and NGS sequencing primers were added during secondary PCR.

Procedures And Architectures
The workflow was designed so that multiplex PCR products are further amplified in a secondary PCR. PCR products were first analyzed by electrophoresis to visualize potential positives. The 172-amplicon panel expected to amplify 28 targets within the plasmids. The full genomes were amplified from 13 nasopharyngeal swab specimens. The specimens were previously diagnosed SARS-CoV-2 positive by RT-PCR. The genomes were sequenced on the Illumina MiSeq. Mutations were detected by two independently developed algorithms. Only mutations detected by both methods were reported. Mutations with %AF > 60% were considered empirically true. Only mutations with %AF ≥ 20% were considered to eliminate noise. Random hexamer-adapters were used to amplify DNA or cDNA targets in the metagenomic method. Background removal reagent was used to remove non-specific amplification products.

Key Results
The mathematical model estimated RT-PCR could detect 4.8 copies at 95% probability. The predicted probability of RT-PCR detecting one copy was 26%. The multiplex PCR panel was estimated to detect 1.15 copies at 95% probability. The two overlapping pools achieved a calculated detection limit of 0.29 copies at 95% probability. The library peaks of expected sizes were obtained from 8,900 to 2.8 copies of plasmids. Quantification demonstrated a wide dynamic range from 1 to about 1,000 copies of plasmids. The library yield started to saturate when the copy number reached 1,700. In practice, a significantly higher 56% probability was observed to detect 1.1 copies. Approximately 96% of the amplicons were recovered with 14 copies of plasmids. About 95% of the genome was covered at 100X for 8 copies of virus. At least 93% of the genome was covered at 100X with 150,000 total reads. At least 58% of the genome was covered at 100X with 50,000 total reads.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The higher experimental detection probability suggests multiplex PCR efficiency is higher than the estimated 6%. The method tolerates the presence of mutations in SARS-CoV-2. The D614G mutation was found in 11 of these 13 specimens. The majority of mutations clustered around 7 loci, reflecting transmission. Low copy number inputs and low read depth may cause false intra-host mutations. The panel specifically amplifies the entire SARS-CoV-2 genome. The metagenomic method achieved >96% coverage of the S and N genes with ~0.6M reads. The viral bases were 16% of the total recovered bases in the sequencing. The method requires no additional means of host depletion to remove human gDNA and rRNA. The panel could be further expanded to include simultaneous detection of other respiratory viruses.

Contradictions And Limitations
No UMI was used in the multiplex PCR amplification. Intra-host mutations might still be contaminated with noise originating from PCR amplification. Some true intra-host mutations with %AF < 20% might be missed. The low detection rate may result from low viral load, timing of sampling, RNA degradation, or primer-binding mutations. The saturation point could be even lower when all 172 amplicons are amplified from positive clinical samples. The metagenomic method requires validation of SARS-CoV-2 and other coronavirus detection. The metagenomic method is economically prohibitive as a diagnostic assay. The occurrence of noise may be exacerbated by low viral copy inputs or low read depth. Recurring mutations in group 2 might not be true intra-host mutations.

Claims
Multiplex PCR is more sensitive than RT-PCR and can detect SARS-CoV-2 at low copy numbers. The multiplex PCR panel was estimated to detect 1.15 copies at 95% probability. The two overlapping pools achieved a calculated detection limit of 0.29 copies at 95% probability. Approximately 96% of the amplicons were recovered with 14 copies of plasmids. The method is more sensitive than RT-PCR and tolerates mutations. No UMI was used in the multiplex PCR amplification. Intra-host mutations might still be contaminated with noise originating from PCR amplification. The method could be further expanded to include simultaneous detection of other respiratory viruses. High-resolution electrophoresis is required to differentiate target amplicons from primer-dimers.
The metagenomic method achieves high coverage of SARS-CoV-2 with modest sequencing depth. The metagenomic method achieved >96% coverage of the S and N genes with ~0.6M reads. The viral bases were 16% of the total recovered bases in the sequencing. This coverage was superior given the recommended 50% threshold of coverage for drafting a genome. The metagenomic method is economically prohibitive as a diagnostic assay. Increasing sequencing depth alone might not improve the coverage of the targeted regions further. The method could be applied for the identification of novel pathogens with a moderate sequencing depth. The results were obtained with no additional means of host depletion to remove human gDNA and rRNA.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The mutations were detected by two independently developed algorithms. Only mutations detected by both methods were reported. The study used a mathematical model to estimate the limit of detection. The study used supplemental figures and tables for additional analyses.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A shows the mathematical model of RT-PCR detection. Figure 1B shows the panel of 172 pairs of multiplex PCR primers. Figure 1C shows the estimated detection limit of 1.15 copies at 95% probability. Figure 2A shows the library peaks of expected sizes from 8,900 to 2.8 copies. Figure 2B shows the wide dynamic range from 1 to about 1,000 copies. Figure 2C shows the 56% probability to detect 1.1 copies. Figure 3A shows the correlation between genome coverage and viral copy number. Figure 3B shows the genome coverage at various total reads. Figure 3E shows the clustering of mutations around 7 loci. Figure 4A shows the 16% of recovered bases within the viral N and S genes. Supplemental Table 2 shows the viral load from 8 to 675,885 RNA copies/uL.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a highly sensitive multiplex PCR method for SARS-CoV-2 detection. 2. The strongest evidence is the calculated detection limit of 0.29 copies at 95% probability. 3. The future path is to expand the panel to include simultaneous detection of other respiratory viruses.
